newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: ADB offers help for India-Bangladesh power link. [CORRECTED 09:21 GMT]
newsitem.headline: ADB offers help for India-Bangladesh power link. [CORRECTED 09:21 GMT]

text.p: The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has offered assistance to Bangladesh for a controversial plan to purchase electrical power from India, government officials said on Thursday.
Bangladesh, suffering a severe power shortfall, is actively considering buying electricity from India as a stand-in measure to boost its power supply.
"The ADB has shown keen interest in sub-regional cooperation in the power sector. They have offered assistance for any such plan," said a Finance Ministry official who asked not to be named.
Government officials said the offer was made by a mission from the Manila-based ADB that visited Bangladesh this week to review progress of bank-funded programmes.

The main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) and some fringe groups, however, have strongly opposed the idea, arguing it would make Bangladesh dependent on India for a key commodity -- electricity.
But Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has said the country will buy electricity from anywhere.
"The government will do everything to get electricity. We will buy electricity from anywhere, maybe from India if prices are cheap and terms respectable," Hasina said last month.

The Energy Ministry says the country currently produces an hourly average (corrects from "a daily average") of about 1,900 megawatts (MW) of electricity against a demand of 2,100 MW, leaving a shortfall of 200 MW.
Energy Minister Nooruddin Khan told a seminar this week that the country's demand for electricity would rise to 3,000 MW by the year 2000 and 4,600 MW by 2005.

Officials said the ADB offered "regional technical assistance" for commercial arrangements between the Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) and the Power Grid Corp of India (PGCI) for setting up a transmission line.
The proposed double circuit line would connect a power substation in Bangladesh's northwestern Jessore district with Jeerhat substation near Calcutta, the capital of India's West Bengal state.
"They (the ADB mission) have also indicated the bank's readiness to fund the installation cost of the 80-km (50 mile) power line," one official said.

The ADB has been one of Bangladesh's leading aid donors, providing $300-400 million in soft loans every year. A government team visited India recently to study the feasibility of importing 100-200 MW of electricity. "We are now working on the findings of the team," one official in Dhaka said.
The shortage of electricity has posed a major hurdle to Bangladesh's plans for rapid industrialisation.

"The power sector suffered criminal neglect in the past...(and) when everything is ready for a take-off, we find there is no electricity," Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria told a foreign investment meeting in Dhaka on Tuesday.
